Good-day to you, sir, and all our dooties to the squire and Cap'n Smollett."”.

questions.prompt: Jim is glad to hear the doctor, but his gladness is “not without admixture.” What is mixed with it?
facilitatorNotes: Shame. He remembers leaving without permission and sees where it has brought him, so he is “ashamed to look him in the face.” The doctor’s “grim nod” shows he is right to expect disapproval.
evidence: I felt ashamed to look him in the face
with one grim nod to me

questions.prompt: The doctor says he will not lose a man “for King George (God bless him!) and the gallows.” What is he really telling his patients?
facilitatorNotes: That he is curing them so they can be tried and hanged. It is a joke with an edge, a “home-thrust,” and the men swallow it in silence. Readers may also see real duty: he treats them carefully whatever they are.
evidence: I make it a point of honour not to lose a man for King George (God bless him!) and the gallows.
The rogues looked at each other, but swallowed the home-thrust in silence.

questions.prompt: Morgan says Dick’s fever “comed of sp'iling Bibles.” What explanation does the doctor give instead, and which one does the evidence support?
facilitatorNotes: The doctor blames their camp in a swamp: they cannot tell “honest air from poison.” The evidence supports a physical cause, since several men are sick, not only Dick. (Mosquitoes, not air, actually spread malaria, so even the doctor’s explanation is only partly right.)
evidence: that comed of sp'iling Bibles
not having sense enough to know honest air from poison

questions.prompt: Why does Silver ask Jim for his “word of honour” before letting him talk to the doctor?
facilitatorNotes: Silver cannot guard Jim and also seem to trust the doctor, so he makes Jim’s promise the guard. Calling him “a young gentleman ... although poor born” flatters Jim into keeping it. It also shows the crew that Silver has not let the hostage go.
evidence: your word of honour not to slip your cable?
for a young gentleman you are, although poor born

readings.title: Treasure Island, chapter XXX — Jim keeps his word
readings.challenge: Decide what a promise is worth when keeping it may cost your life.
readings.focus: Given a chance to escape, Jim refuses to break his parole, and the doctor discovers how much the boy has done.
readings.context: Recap: Dr. Livesey came to the pirates’ camp to treat their fevers. He asked to talk with Jim, and Silver, against the crew’s protests, allowed it once Jim gave his word of honour not to escape. Parole is a prisoner’s promise not to run away. To gammon is to fool; chuck-farthing is a gambling game of tossing coins; “holus bolus” means all at once; perjury is lying under oath in court; to have one’s “wig sorted” is to be scolded; a squall is a sudden storm.
readings.contentNote: Jim says his life is forfeit and that what he fears is torture.

excerpt.locator: Part VI, “Captain Silver”: Chapter XXX, “On Parole,” from the crew’s anger at Silver to the end of the chapter; opens “The explosion of disapproval, which nothing but Silver's black looks had restrained,…”; closes “…me through the stockade, nodded to Silver, and set off at a brisk pace into the wood.”.

questions.prompt: The crew accuse Silver “of the identical, exact thing that he was doing.” How does he still win the argument?
facilitatorNotes: By force of personality: he calls them fools, waves the chart, and promises that they will break the treaty themselves “when the time comes.” Jim says they were “silenced by his volubility rather than convinced,” which suggests the victory may not last.
evidence: it's us must break the treaty when the time comes
silenced by his volubility rather than convinced

questions.prompt: Out of the crew’s sight, Silver seems “a changed man.” Is his fear real, or another performance?
facilitatorNotes: His face and voice change and he admits “the shakes ... for the gallows.” Jim believes it: “never was a soul more dead in earnest.” Readers may still note that Silver times everything and makes sure the doctor will “put that down” for him; both can be true.
evidence: never was a soul more dead in earnest
I've the shakes upon me for the gallows

questions.prompt: The doctor urges Jim to jump the fence and run. Why does Jim refuse, and do you think he is right?
facilitatorNotes: He has given his word, Silver trusted him, and he says none of his friends would break theirs either. Some readers will admire the choice; others will say a promise to a pirate holding him prisoner does not bind him. The doctor himself offers to take the “blame and shame.”
evidence: Silver trusted me; I passed my word, and back I go.
you know right well you wouldn't do the thing yourself

questions.prompt: What does the doctor seem to know that Jim and Silver do not? How does Stevenson let us see that he knows something without telling us what?
facilitatorNotes: He mentions Ben Gunn suddenly, warns Silver not to hurry after the treasure and to “look out for squalls,” and says the secret is not his to tell. The reader, like Silver, gets hints but no answer. Readers can connect this with the chart given away in Chapter XXVIII.
evidence: don't you be in any great hurry after that treasure
it's not my secret, you see, Silver

readings.title: Treasure Island, chapter XXXI — A foot in either camp
readings.challenge: Compare what Silver tells Jim in private with what he tells the crew in public, and decide which to believe.
readings.focus: Setting out on the treasure hunt as Silver’s hostage, Jim sees that the man protecting him may betray him at any moment.
readings.context: Treasure Island (1883) is Robert Louis Stevenson’s novel of a hunt for pirate gold, told by Jim Hawkins, who looks back on adventures from his boyhood. Near the end of the book, the pirates hold the stockade and Jim is their prisoner. Long John Silver has saved him from the crew in exchange for Jim’s promise to speak for him if they are tried for piracy. Dr. Livesey, who earlier gave Silver the treasure map for reasons no one understands, visited the camp; he urged Jim to escape, but Jim had given his word and would not. The doctor warned Silver to “look out for squalls” when he found the treasure. Sealed orders are orders not to be opened until a set time; junk is salt meat; windward is the side the wind comes from; a brush is a short fight; gigs are a ship’s small boats, a thwart is a rowing seat, and “unbaled” means not bailed out; burthened means burdened.

excerpt.locator: Part VI, “Captain Silver”: Chapter XXXI, “The Treasure Hunt—Flint’s Pointer,” from the start to the party setting out in the two gigs; opens “"Jim," said Silver, when we were alone, "if I saved your life, you saved mine; and I'll…”; closes “…so, with our numbers divided between them, we set forth upon the bosom of the anchorage.”.

questions.prompt: What does Jim notice about the way the pirates cook and eat? What does he conclude from it?
facilitatorNotes: They build a huge fire, cook three times what they can eat and throw the rest in the flames. Jim concludes they live “hand to mouth” and could fight a short battle but never a long campaign: an observation used as evidence.
evidence: I never in my life saw men so careless of the morrow
their entire unfitness for anything like a prolonged campaign

questions.prompt: Silver promised Jim they would stick “back to back.” What does he tell the crew about Jim at breakfast, and which version does Jim believe?
facilitatorNotes: To the crew Jim is a hostage to be kept “like so much gold” and later talked over. Jim believes Silver would take the pirates’ side if it worked, because wealth and freedom beat “a bare escape from hanging.” Readers may think Silver is only calming the crew; Jim admits he cannot be sure.
evidence: we'll keep him like so much gold, in case of accidents
He had still a foot in either camp

questions.prompt: Even if Silver keeps faith with the doctor, Jim sees danger ahead. What is it?
facilitatorNotes: If the crew find out, Silver and Jim must fight five strong men alone: “he, a cripple, and I, a boy.” Jim adds the mystery of his friends’ behaviour, so he sets out with three fears at once.
evidence: he, a cripple, and I, a boy--against five strong and active seamen!
how little taste I found in my breakfast

questions.prompt: Jim says he was “led like a dancing bear.” What picture does that give of him and Silver as they set out?
facilitatorNotes: Jim walks on a rope whose end Silver holds, sometimes in his teeth, while the parrot chatters on Silver’s armed shoulder: Jim is a captive on show. The image also makes Silver the showman, which suits a man who performs for every audience.
evidence: For all the world, I was led like a dancing bear.
now between his powerful teeth

readings.title: Treasure Island, chapter XXXI — Flint’s pointer
readings.challenge: Use the clues around a skeleton to test the pirates’ explanation of it.
readings.focus: The treasure hunters find one of Flint’s victims laid out as a signpost, and fear of the dead captain spreads through the party.
readings.context: Recap: the pirates set out to find Flint’s treasure, with Jim tied by a rope to Silver, who may betray either side. Jim suspects Silver will turn on his friends if he can seize both treasure and ship. The note on the back of Flint’s chart gives compass directions (N.N.E. is north-north-east; E.S.E. is east-south-east); a bearing is a direction measured with a compass. Marish means marshy; broom is a flowering shrub; deadlights are eyes; coins were laid on a dead man’s eyes; a sperrit is a spirit or ghost; doubloons are gold coins, a doit is a tiny one, and a baccy-box holds tobacco; “Care killed a cat” means worry does harm; with bated breath means almost whispering. Captain Flint, the pirate who buried the treasure, died at Savannah in Georgia.
readings.contentNote: The party finds a skeleton; the pirates say Flint murdered his six shipmates and describe his drunken death.

excerpt.locator: Part VI, “Captain Silver”: Chapter XXXI, “The Treasure Hunt—Flint’s Pointer,” from the discussion of the chart to the end of the chapter; opens “As we pulled over, there was some discussion on the chart. The red cross was, of course,…”; closes “…spoke with bated breath. The terror of the dead buccaneer had fallen on their spirits.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the note on the back of the chart hard to follow? What can only be settled on the spot?
facilitatorNotes: The red cross is too big to guide them, and the plateau has several tall trees standing above the rest. Only compass readings taken on the ground can say which one Flint meant; until then, every man picks “a favourite of his own.”
evidence: admitted of some ambiguity
could only be decided on the spot, and by the readings of the compass

questions.prompt: How does Silver work out what the skeleton is for? What does he notice that the others do not?
facilitatorNotes: He sees that the body lies too straight, feet one way and arms over the head “like a diver's,” and checks it with the compass. It points exactly along Flint’s bearing: “a p'inter.” He reasons from an odd detail to a purpose.
evidence: what sort of a way is that for bones to lie? 'Tain't in natur'.
this here is a p'inter.

questions.prompt: The men notice that the dead man has no knife, no coin, not even a tobacco box. What might explain that, and why do they not follow the clue?
facilitatorNotes: Someone has been there since Flint and taken them. The pirates feel it is not “nat'ral” but quickly turn to talk of ghosts instead of asking who. Readers may remember who else lives on the island and keep the clue for later.
evidence: why don't we find his'n lying round?
not a copper doit nor a baccy-box

questions.prompt: How does the mood of the party change between the climb and the end of the chapter?
facilitatorNotes: They begin by spreading out in a fan, shouting and leaping in the fresh air; after the skeleton and the talk of Flint they walk “side by side” and whisper. Silver’s joke that Flint “won't walk by day” shows that even he admits the fear.
evidence: shouting and leaping to and fro
kept side by side and spoke with bated breath

readings.title: Treasure Island, chapter XXXII — The voice among the trees
readings.challenge: Notice how one sound can mean different things to different listeners, and look for the explanation behind it.
readings.focus: A voice from the woods nearly breaks the pirates; greed drives them on, straight to an empty pit.
readings.context: Recap: climbing to the plateau, the treasure hunters found a skeleton laid out by Flint to point towards the treasure, and fell to whispering about Flint’s murders and his death. Jim is still tied to Silver. “Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest” is the pirates’ song, which Billy Bones sang at the inn in Chapter I; skylarking is playing tricks; to “fetch aft” is to bring to the back of the ship; to “show his stern” is to run away; boosy means drunk and a mug is a face; “’Bout ship” means turn the ship around; a cache is a hiding place, and rifled means robbed; “clear to probation” means proved beyond doubt. Ben Gunn, a pirate marooned on the island three years before, once sailed with Flint.
readings.contentNote: Silver looks at Jim murderously; Jim imagines Flint killing his six shipmates on the same spot.

excerpt.locator: Part VI, “Captain Silver”: Chapter XXXII, “The Treasure Hunt—The Voice Among the Trees,” the whole chapter; opens “Partly from the damping influence of this alarm, partly to rest Silver and the sick folk,…”; closes “…The _cache_ had been found and rifled: the seven hundred thousand pounds were gone!”.

questions.prompt: The pirates go white at the singing, but Jim thinks it sounded “airily and sweetly.” Why does the same sound affect them so differently?
facilitatorNotes: The pirates knew Flint and his song, and have just been talking of his death; Jim hears only a voice in the sunshine. Fear lives in the listener’s memory as much as in the sound. Jim calls the effect on the men “the stranger” for that reason.
evidence: I thought it had sounded airily and sweetly; and the effect on my companions was the stranger.
The colour went from their six faces like enchantment

questions.prompt: Silver argues that a spirit cannot have an echo. Jim calls this “weak enough.” Why does it work anyway, and what clue had Silver already noticed?
facilitatorNotes: Superstitious men need an argument in the language of superstition, and Silver gives them one. The better clue is that no one on the island had ever heard of Darby “but us that's here,” so the voice belongs to someone who sailed with Flint, which leads to Ben Gunn.
evidence: This argument seemed weak enough to me.
Nobody in this here island ever heard of Darby

questions.prompt: “Dead or alive, nobody minded Ben Gunn.” Why might the narrator repeat this line? Is it true?
facilitatorNotes: The pirates are relieved because they despise Ben Gunn. Jim repeats it flatly, and a reader who remembers meeting Ben Gunn may hear warning in it: the man nobody minds has been ahead of them all along. Some readers will hear plain description, others irony; the chapter’s last lines favour irony.
evidence: Why, nobody minds Ben Gunn
He had said the truth; dead or alive, nobody minded Ben Gunn.

questions.prompt: What does Jim “read like print” in Silver’s face as the gold comes near? How certain can he be?
facilitatorNotes: That Silver has forgotten his promise and means to take the treasure and the ship and “cut every honest throat.” Jim reads it from Silver’s tugging at the rope and his deadly looks; it is a strong inference, not proof, and the next moment, at the empty pit, makes it impossible to test.
evidence: certainly I read them like print
his promise and the doctor's warning were both things of the past

readings.title: Treasure Island, chapter XXXIII — The fall of a chieftain
readings.challenge: Fit the doctor’s explanation to the mysteries of the last several chapters, one by one.
readings.focus: Silver changes sides in a second, the doctor’s ambush ends the mutiny, and the secret of the treasure is told.
readings.context: Recap: led on by the treasure map, the pirates reached Flint’s tall tree after a voice that sounded like Flint’s dead self, or like Ben Gunn’s, had nearly sent them running. They found a great hole, broken boards marked with the name of Flint’s ship, the Walrus, and no treasure. A guinea is a gold coin; pig-nuts are edible roots; a teetotum is a spinning top; a maroon is someone left alone on an island; to prosecute is to bring to trial; a millstone round the neck is a heavy burden of guilt (an image from the Bible); dereliction of duty is failing to do it; quadrilaterals are four-sided shapes, here gold bars; to scuttle a ship is to sink it on purpose; obsequious means too eager to please.
readings.contentNote: Two pirates are shot dead from ambush; Silver fires his pistol into the wounded George Merry.

excerpt.locator: Part VI, “Captain Silver”: Chapter XXXIII, “The Fall of a Chieftain,” the whole chapter; opens “There never was such an overturn in this world. Each of these six men was as though he…”; closes “…quietly in our laughter--the same bland, polite, obsequious seaman of the voyage out.”.

questions.prompt: Jim whispers, “So you've changed sides again.” Is he fair to Silver? How does Jim seem to feel about him a moment later?
facilitatorNotes: He is accurate and “revolted.” Yet as Silver stands alone facing five men, Jim admits, “He was brave, and no mistake.” Jim keeps judging Silver and admiring him at once, and the chapter lets both stand.
evidence: I was so revolted at these constant changes
He was brave, and no mistake.

questions.prompt: Silver shoots the wounded Merry and says, “George, I reckon I settled you.” What does this moment show, just as he joins the honest side?
facilitatorNotes: That he has not changed at all: quick, ruthless and settling an old score. Readers may see it as proof of loyalty to his new side, as revenge on the man who deposed him, or as both. The cold remark makes it hard to like him even as he helps Jim.
evidence: Long John had fired two barrels of a pistol into the struggling Merry
I reckon I settled you.

questions.prompt: The doctor’s story explains several mysteries. Which ones, and how?
facilitatorNotes: Ben Gunn had found and moved the treasure, so the chart was “now useless,” which is why the doctor gave it away with the stockade and stores; the warning about squalls meant the empty pit; the voice in the trees was Ben Gunn playing on the pirates’ fears. Ask which explanation readers had guessed.
evidence: given him the chart, which was now useless
Then it had occurred to him to work upon the superstitions of his former shipmates

questions.prompt: When Jim at last sees the treasure, he stops to count what it cost. Why does he do this at the moment of success?
facilitatorNotes: The sight makes him think of everything behind it: seventeen men dead on this voyage and countless “brave men walking the plank” before. The treasure becomes a record of crimes, not only a prize. Some readers feel the joy of the supper that follows is shadowed by this paragraph; others feel it earns the rest.
evidence: that had cost already the lives of seventeen men
what shame and lies and cruelty, perhaps no man alive could tell

readings.title: Treasure Island, chapter XXXIV — And last
readings.challenge: Judge the endings the narrator gives each character, and ask what the final lines leave in the reader’s ear.
readings.focus: The treasure is loaded, three mutineers are left behind, Silver slips away, and Jim says what the adventure left him.
readings.context: Recap: Ben Gunn had moved Flint’s treasure to his cave long before; the doctor’s ambush killed two of the pirates and scattered three more, and Silver, back on the honest side, was spared prosecution. The friends, with the treasure, are reunited in Ben Gunn’s cave. Georges and Louises are English and French coins named after kings; doubloons, moidores and sequins are Spanish, Portuguese and Venetian gold coins; to ingratiate oneself is to try to win favour; “hand and glove” means close partners; supplication is begging; a man-of-war is a warship; to connive is to secretly help; a bulkhead is a wall inside a ship; to be “smit” is to be struck; a butt is the target of jokes; a wain is a farm wagon.
readings.contentNote: Three mutineers are left on the island, begging not to be abandoned, and one fires at the ship. The narrator uses words for Black and mixed-race people that were common in 1880s Britain and are offensive today.

excerpt.locator: Part VI, “Captain Silver”: Chapter XXXIV, “And Last,” the whole chapter, to the end of the novel; opens “The next morning we fell early to work, for the transportation of this great mass of gold…”; closes “…voice of Captain Flint still ringing in my ears: "Pieces of eight! pieces of eight!"”.

questions.prompt: Jim says sorting the coins gave him more pleasure than anything. What does his description of them show about the treasure, and about Jim?
facilitatorNotes: The coins come from every nation and the last hundred years: the treasure is the loot of a century of piracy. Jim enjoys their variety and strangeness, “like autumn leaves,” more than their worth. Ask what else autumn leaves suggest.
evidence: the pictures of all the kings of Europe for the last hundred years
they were like autumn leaves

questions.prompt: Was it right to leave the three mutineers on the island? What reasons does Jim give, and what makes the scene hard to read?
facilitatorNotes: They could not risk another mutiny, and taking them home to be hanged would be “a cruel sort of kindness”; stores and medicine were left. But the men kneel and beg “for God's sake,” and one fires a shot. Students may judge it merciful, practical, or cruel.
evidence: to take them home for the gibbet would have been a cruel sort of kindness
appeal to us, for God's sake, to be merciful

questions.prompt: Silver escapes with a bag of coin instead of being hanged. How does Jim feel about it, and why might Stevenson end Silver’s story this way?
facilitatorNotes: Jim and his friends are “pleased to be so cheaply quit of him,” and Jim even hopes Silver lives in comfort, though he doubts his soul. Stevenson keeps Silver as he has been all along: impossible to pin down. Some readers want justice; others are glad he is free.
evidence: I think we were all pleased to be so cheaply quit of him.
his chances of comfort in another world are very small

questions.prompt: The novel ends not with riches but with Jim’s bad dreams and the parrot’s cry. What does the adventure seem to have left him?
facilitatorNotes: He would not go back for the rest of the silver for anything; the island is “accursed,” and the parrot’s voice still wakes him. The ending turns a treasure story into a memory of fear and loss. Readers may also hear a storyteller’s pleasure in the last ringing words.
evidence: Oxen and wain-ropes would not bring me back again to that accursed island
Pieces of eight! pieces of eight!

readings.title: Will o’ the Mill, part I — Everything goes downward
readings.challenge: Follow long, rolling sentences and collect the details that all point one way.
readings.focus: A boy in a mountain valley notices that everything he sees is going down towards a world he has never seen, and is seized by longing for it.
readings.context: Robert Louis Stevenson published “Will o’ the Mill” in the Cornhill Magazine in 1878, five years before Treasure Island; the 1911 Swanston Edition prints it after the novel. It is a story in three parts about a man who must choose between going out into the world and staying where he is. Will, an orphan, is raised by a miller and his wife in a mill on a mountain road. An eminence is a hilltop; a pass is a way over the mountains; a thoroughfare is a busy road; a tumbril is a cart and regimentals are uniforms; a barouche is a carriage, and the dicky is the servants’ seat on it; a stock is a post or stump; a weir is a low dam; sixscore is 120; solicitations are urgings. Stevenson’s sentences are long and musical, so reading parts aloud helps.
readings.contentNote: An army marches past the mill to a war; none of the soldiers return.

excerpt.locator: “Will o’ the Mill,” Part I, “The Plain and the Stars,” from the start to Will’s longing for everything that went down the valley; opens “The Mill where Will lived with his adopted parents stood in a falling valley between…”; closes “…brown water in the stream, he felt his heart flow out after it in an ecstasy of longing.”.

questions.prompt: What does Will notice about the direction in which things travel past the mill? Find at least three examples.
facilitatorNotes: Carriages (“five-sixths were plunging briskly downwards”), walkers and pedlars, the army, the river, even the wind and the dead leaves all go down the valley. Only the fish keep their heads upstream, which is why Will feels they “stood faithfully by him.”
evidence: five-sixths were plunging briskly downwards and only one-sixth crawling up
they all went downward, fleetly and gaily downward

questions.prompt: The army that marches past never comes back. What does the boy feel as he watches it, and how does this sight feed his question “Whither”?
facilitatorNotes: He feels “weariness, pity, and wonder” at the tired soldiers, and notices that “not a man returned.” Everything that goes down the valley disappears into the unknown. Some readers will feel only mystery here; others will sense that “downward” can also mean towards death.
evidence: filled him with a sense of weariness, pity, and wonder
Will saw one thing plainly, that not a man returned.

questions.prompt: How does the miller describe the sea? Which parts sound like fact and which like tales he has heard?
facilitatorNotes: Fact: rivers run into a great salt lake, storms raise huge waves, ships come from the Indies. Tale: fish “five times bigger than a bull” (perhaps whales) and a crowned sea serpent. His repeated “they say” shows that he has never seen it either.
evidence: it is the greatest thing God made
one old serpent as long as our river and as old as all the world

questions.prompt: Why does Will burst into tears when he first sees the whole plain from the hill-top? Why is the miller disappointed?
facilitatorNotes: The sight is too large for him; an “overmastering emotion” takes his breath away. It may be joy, longing, or the pain of seeing what he cannot reach. The miller meant to give him a treat and does not understand what he has started.
evidence: An overmastering emotion seized upon the boy, soul and body
the poor miller, sadly disappointed and perplexed

readings.title: Will o’ the Mill, part I — The divine unrest
readings.challenge: Follow the narrator when he leaves the story to argue an idea, and find how the argument returns to Will.
readings.focus: The narrator calls Will’s longing a “divine unrest” that drives explorers and pilgrims, and then turns the mill into an inn where the world comes to Will’s door.
readings.context: Recap: Will, raised by the miller in a mountain valley, has noticed that everything on the road and river goes down towards the plain. The miller’s tales and a view of the whole plain from the hill-top have filled him with longing to follow them. Abstruse means hard to understand; “supply and demand” is an idea from economics; the tribes “out of the North and East” are the peoples who moved into the Roman Empire long ago, and the Eternal City is Rome; in Greek myth Icarus flew on wings of wax until he fell; purged means cleansed; jocund means merry; variegated means many-coloured; a publican is an innkeeper; a post-master kept the station where coach horses were changed; an equipage is a carriage with its horses and servants.

excerpt.locator: “Will o’ the Mill,” Part I, “The Plain and the Stars,” from the narrator’s reflection on wanderers to Will’s dream of a waiting carriage; opens “We are told by men of science that all the ventures of mariners on the sea, all that…”; closes “…equipage occupied a place in his mind as something to be both feared and hoped for.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator argues with “men of science” about why people have always wandered. What explanation does he reject, and what does he put in its place?
facilitatorNotes: He rejects the idea that they moved only for food and trade, “a dull and pitiful explanation.” He says they were pilgrims driven by a “divine unrest” that makes both great achievements and miserable failures. Students can say which explanation they find more convincing, or whether both can be true.
evidence: a certain natural instinct for cheap rations
That divine unrest, that old stinging trouble of humanity

questions.prompt: What does the legend of the old man shod with iron suggest about longing?
facilitatorNotes: He has worn out three pairs of iron shoes looking for the Eternal City and has not found it. Longing may never reach its goal, and the searchers keep going anyway. Readers may see a warning for Will, or simply a picture of how strong the urge is.
evidence: And all this while I have not found the city.

questions.prompt: The narrator says Will was “sick as if for home,” then corrects himself: “the figure halts.” Why is homesickness not quite the right comparison?
facilitatorNotes: Homesickness is for a place you have known; Will longs for a life he has never had. So the narrator reaches for a stranger picture: someone not yet born, stretching out his hands towards life. Ask what “many-coloured, many-sounding” adds.
evidence: I have said he was sick as if for home: the figure halts.
stretching out his hands lovingly towards many-coloured, many-sounding life

questions.prompt: Will dreams night after night of a carriage waiting to take him to the plain. Why might the dream change from “all jollity” to something “feared and hoped for”?
facilitatorNotes: The longer he waits, the more serious leaving becomes: it would mean leaving everything he knows. Readers can predict whether the carriage will ever come and what it might be; keep the predictions to check later in the story.
evidence: a splendid equipage waited at the door to carry him down into the plain
something to be both feared and hoped for

readings.title: Will o’ the Mill, part I — The plain and the stars
readings.challenge: Turn a comparison into an argument: say what the stars are meant to prove.
readings.focus: A cheerful traveller answers Will’s longing with a parable of the stars, and Will draws a gloomy conclusion from it.
readings.context: Recap: Will, raised in a mill in a mountain valley, has always longed to go down to the cities of the plain. The mill has become a wayside inn, and Will waits on travellers and questions them about the world. Hipped means low-spirited; Arcturus and Aldebaran are bright stars; a parable is a story that teaches by comparison; “the mountain and the mouse” recalls the fable of a mountain that groaned and gave birth to a mouse.
readings.contentNote: The traveller says that cities are so hard on the poor that many take their own lives.

excerpt.locator: “Will o’ the Mill,” Part I, “The Plain and the Stars,” from the fat young man’s arrival to the end of Part I; opens “One day, when Will was about sixteen, a fat young man arrived at sunset to pass the…”; closes “…philosophically over his nuts? I needn't ask you which of them looked more of a fool."”.

questions.prompt: The young man warns that people in the plain are unhappy too. How does Will answer, and what does his answer show he has learned?
facilitatorNotes: He has “used his eyes”: he knows that nature and people live on one another, and that the shepherd carries the lamb home to eat it. He no longer expects a perfect world; he wants to live and see, “let it be good or evil.”
evidence: Although I have never been out of this valley, believe me, I have used my eyes.
the shepherd, who makes so pretty a picture carrying home the lamb, is only carrying it home for dinner

questions.prompt: “Thousands of people live and die like you,” says the young man. Is Will’s reply a good one?
facilitatorNotes: Will says that if thousands would like his life, one of them can have his place. It is quick and fair: contentment that suits others does not suit him. Some readers will side with the traveller, who means that a quiet life can be happy.
evidence: if there are thousands who would like, why should not one of them have my place?

questions.prompt: Explain the young man’s parable of the stars in your own words. Why does he say a parable is “not the same thing as a reason”?
facilitatorNotes: The stars may hold answers to all our troubles, yet no one can ever reach them: all we can do is admire them. So too, perhaps, with the plain. A parable persuades by a picture rather than by proof, which he admits is “usually vastly more convincing.” Ask whether that is fair.
evidence: We may climb the highest mountain, and we are no nearer them.
It is not the same thing as a reason, but usually vastly more convincing.

questions.prompt: Will concludes, “We are in a rat-trap.” Which of the two squirrels does the young man think wiser, and do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: The one “sitting philosophically over his nuts”: if you cannot escape the cage, enjoy what you have. Will hears only the trap. Students may admire the calm squirrel or defend the one that keeps turning; the rest of the story tests this advice.
evidence: We are in a rat-trap.
another squirrel sitting philosophically over his nuts

readings.title: Will o’ the Mill, part II — The parson’s Marjory
readings.challenge: Notice how a character’s way of seeing changes the whole landscape around him.
readings.focus: Will, now a grown innkeeper who has never left his valley, falls in love, and feels for the first time that he need not go anywhere.
readings.context: Robert Louis Stevenson’s story “Will o’ the Mill” (1878) has three parts. In Part I, “The Plain and the Stars,” Will grew up in a mountain mill and longed to follow the river down to the cities of the plain. A traveller showed him the stars, which no one can reach, and compared restless longing to a squirrel turning in a cage. Part II begins some years later. Inscrutable means hard to read; “six feet three in his stockings” is his height without shoes; a constitution is a person’s health; a parson is a village clergyman and the parsonage his house; a “man of substance” is well-off; cajoled means coaxed; to “rule the roast” is to be in charge; beatitude is deep happiness; a wimple here is a ripple.

excerpt.locator: “Will o’ the Mill,” Part II, “The Parson’s Marjory,” from the start to Will’s thoughts on the hill-top; opens “After some years the old people died, both in one winter, very carefully tended by their…”; closes “…waiting patiently in his own narrow valley, he also had attained the better sunlight.”.

questions.prompt: People expected Will to sell the mill and go down the river when the old couple died. What does he do instead, and how do the neighbours see him?
facilitatorNotes: He stays, improves the inn and settles down, “a kind, talkative, inscrutable young man.” The neighbours think him “a bit of an oddity” because he questions plain common sense. Ask why the narrator calls his courtship the oddest thing of all.
evidence: But there was never any sign of such an intention on the part of Will.
a bit of an oddity

questions.prompt: Gossips say the parson and his daughter chose Will’s inn on purpose. Does the narrator agree?
facilitatorNotes: No: the gossip comes from “ill-wishers,” and Marjory comes “with the most unshaken innocence and unconcern.” The narrator also hints that Marjory may be as steady as Will, which prepares for what follows.
evidence: among their ill-wishers
with the most unshaken innocence and unconcern

questions.prompt: When Will looks at Marjory, what happens to the rest of the valley in his eyes?
facilitatorNotes: Everything else goes dull: the trees “inanimate,” the clouds “like dead things,” the mountains “disenchanted.” The landscape that once pointed him towards the plain now fades beside one person. Ask whether this is love, or a new kind of longing.
evidence: the clouds hung in heaven like dead things
The whole valley could not compare in looks with this one girl.

questions.prompt: On the hill-top above the plain, Will decides that the river and the birds are “empty bustle.” What has he found instead, and how does it answer his boyhood longing?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks he has reached the “better sunlight” without leaving: what he longed to find in the plain has come to him. Readers can decide whether this is wisdom or a new illusion; the next nights test it.
evidence: he also had attained the better sunlight
without stirring a foot, waiting patiently in his own narrow valley

readings.title: Will o’ the Mill, part II — Flowers and stars
readings.challenge: Follow a conversation about flowers that is really about something else.
readings.focus: Will declares his love and becomes engaged, then talks himself, through an argument about picking flowers, into doubting that he should marry at all.
readings.context: Recap: Will, who has never left his mountain valley, now keeps the inn there. The parson and his daughter Marjory are lodging with him while their house is repaired, and Will has fallen deeply in love with her. A declaration is a confession of love; to commit oneself is to make a promise; Madge is a pet name for Marjory; indispensable means necessary; in the fable, a farmer kills the goose that lays golden eggs to get all the gold at once, and loses everything; “even” is evening; populous means crowded.

excerpt.locator: “Will o’ the Mill,” Part II, “The Parson’s Marjory,” from Will’s declaration to his night in the garden; opens “The next day Will made a sort of declaration across the dinner-table, while the parson…”; closes “…in a pretty way?" And he went off to bed, chuckling to himself: "If I were only a fool!"”.

questions.prompt: How does Will declare his love? What is odd about the way he does it?
facilitatorNotes: He says he does not want to be held to it, “for I may be wrong,” and asks Marjory to shake her head if she disagrees. He speaks almost like a scientist reporting a finding. Her answer, “I think I do,” is just as uncertain, and the parson settles everything in four words.
evidence: I do not wish to be held as committing myself
I fancy I must be what they call in love

questions.prompt: After the engagement, Will seems to avoid Marjory. Does he care less for her?
facilitatorNotes: No: “she was never out of Will's mind for an instant,” and the whole world looks new to him. He enjoys thinking of her more than being with her, which the narrator says may have disappointed her. This is the first sign of how he will act.
evidence: she was never out of Will's mind for an instant
it seemed as if he avoided her rather than sought her out

questions.prompt: Marjory picks flowers to keep them; Will says she does it “in order to think no more about them.” How does he connect this with his boyhood wish, and what does he suddenly realise?
facilitatorNotes: Going down to the plain would have meant losing the view of it; picking the flower ends the charm. His sudden “By the Lord!” suggests he sees that marrying Marjory might be the same: possessing her would end the wonder. Readers may find the argument wise or chilly.
evidence: in order to think no more about them
Because I had a fancy for looking out over the plain, I wished to go down there--where I couldn't look out over it any longer.

questions.prompt: That night Will laughs, “If I were only a fool!” What does he mean? Is he wise or foolish here?
facilitatorNotes: He means a fool would simply marry her; he, the thinker, will keep both Marjory and the stars at a distance and admire them. The lifted blind suggests Marjory is watching too, and the reader may suspect that his cleverness is the real foolishness. Both readings can be supported.
evidence: There she is in her room," he thought, "and there are the stars overhead
If I were only a fool!

readings.title: Will o’ the Mill, part II — Not worth while
readings.challenge: Read two people’s words for what each of them hides.
readings.focus: Will tells Marjory that marriage is not worth while; she answers by taking charge, and he discovers that he did not understand her at all.
readings.context: Recap: Will declared his love and Marjory accepted him, but in a talk about picking flowers he decided that possessing a thing ends the pleasure of wondering at it. That night he resolved to keep Marjory, like the stars, at a distance. To be disconcerted is to be thrown off balance; “fancy-free” means not in love; “a clean shrift” is an honest confession; dubiety is doubt and perturbation is agitation; inmates here are lodgers; to be put “out of countenance” is to be embarrassed; crestfallen means disappointed; dexterity is skill; perverse means contrary.

excerpt.locator: “Will o’ the Mill,” Part II, “The Parson’s Marjory,” from Will’s announcement in the garden to Marjory’s departure and his confusion; opens “The next morning, pretty early, he saw her once more in the garden, and sought her out.”; closes “…man who has lived among shadows and now meets the sun, he was both pained and delighted.”.

questions.prompt: How does Will tell Marjory he has changed his mind? Why does she call it an insult?
facilitatorNotes: He announces cheerfully that marriage is “not worth while,” proposes that he visit her “as people go to church,” and then offers to marry her anyway. Offering marriage as a favour he thinks unwise is what insults her.
evidence: I have made up my mind it's not worth while.
Do you know that you are insulting me?

questions.prompt: Will asks, “Can a man be more downright or honourable to a woman than I have been?” What is your answer?
facilitatorNotes: He has been honest and has offered her a choice. But he cannot see how his honesty hurts: he notices her tremble, then grows angry when she will not speak. Students may defend him as honest or blame him as blind to her feelings.
evidence: Can a man be more downright or honourable to a woman than I have been?
He could see her tremble.

questions.prompt: At dinner, Marjory tells her father what happened. What does she change in the story, and why?
facilitatorNotes: She says Will gave up the marriage “at my request,” and stops him from correcting her. Taking the decision as her own protects her pride and shows a strength Will had not suspected. Readers may admire her or think she is hiding her hurt.
evidence: he has agreed, at my request, to give up all idea of marriage
to let me explain these matters for myself

questions.prompt: After she leaves, Will is “both pained and delighted.” What has he discovered in Marjory, and why does it trouble him?
facilitatorNotes: A “fine, perverse angel” in her quiet soul: a will as strong as his. It does not fit his “life of artificial calm,” yet he wants it badly. The narrator’s word “artificial” suggests his calm was never as natural as he thought.
evidence: He thought he recognised a fine, perverse angel in that still soul
Like a man who has lived among shadows and now meets the sun

readings.title: Will o’ the Mill, part II — Will o’ the Mill’s Corner
readings.challenge: Compare what a character says about his feelings with what the narrator shows.
readings.focus: Will goes to propose again, lets himself be turned aside, and keeps his distance for years until it is too late.
readings.context: Recap: Will told Marjory that marriage was not worth while, and she took charge, telling her father that the decision was hers and leaving the inn. Will was left lonely and confused, admiring her more than ever. To plume oneself is to be proud; tenor is the usual course of thought; a thorn switch is a walking stick; “infirmity of purpose” is weakness of will; to whet the appetite is to sharpen it; “affected” here means was fond of; to moralise is to reflect on right and wrong; fickle means changeable; “fell away in flesh” means grew thin.
readings.contentNote: Marjory dies young, a year after her marriage; Will weeps at her bedside.

excerpt.locator: “Will o’ the Mill,” Part II, “The Parson’s Marjory,” from Will’s walk down the valley to the end of Part II; opens “As the days went forward he passed from one extreme to another; now pluming himself on…”; closes “…talk in private, and he was present and wept very bitterly while she breathed her last.”.

questions.prompt: Walking down the valley to propose, what answer does Will hope for? Why does his wish keep changing?
facilitatorNotes: He hopes “on the whole” she will refuse, so that he can keep his calm with a clear conscience; then, seeing her roof, he half wants her to accept. He is ashamed of his own “infirmity of purpose.” The man who knew his own mind no longer does.
evidence: He hoped, on the whole, she would refuse him
more than half-ashamed of himself for this infirmity of purpose

questions.prompt: Marjory interrupts Will’s “At the same time----” and praises his wisdom. Why might she stop him from finishing?
facilitatorNotes: She may truly agree; she may be protecting her pride after being refused once; or she may be testing him. Will takes her words at face value (“It appears I was right after all”). The narrator does not tell us, and the end of the part makes her words harder to believe.
evidence: You understood me better than I understood myself
It appears I was right after all.

questions.prompt: Why does Will often walk half-way to the parsonage and then turn back? How does this fit his ideas from earlier in the story?
facilitatorNotes: He rations his pleasure “as if to whet his appetite,” keeping Marjory, like the plain and the stars, a thing to look at from a distance. His favourite corner even shows the spire with a “snatch of plain” behind it. Ask whether this is happiness or avoidance.
evidence: as if to whet his appetite
with a triangular snatch of plain by way of background

questions.prompt: When Marjory marries someone else, Will says he has had an escape. Does the narrator believe him? What does the last scene show?
facilitatorNotes: No: “at heart he was reasonably displeased,” moped and grew thin. At her deathbed he “wept very bitterly.” His wise sayings cover a real loss. Some readers will pity Will; others will say he chose this.
evidence: But at heart he was reasonably displeased
wept very bitterly while she breathed her last

readings.title: Will o’ the Mill, part III — A night of memories
readings.challenge: Notice how details from earlier in a story return with new meaning.
readings.focus: Will grows old and famous for his wisdom without leaving his valley; one stormy night his whole past seems to come back to him.
readings.context: Robert Louis Stevenson’s story “Will o’ the Mill” (1878) has three parts. In Part I, Will grew up in a mountain mill longing to follow the river to the cities of the plain, until a traveller persuaded him that such longing is like a squirrel turning in a cage. In Part II he fell in love with the parson’s daughter, Marjory, but decided that marriage was “not worth while”; for three years he visited her once or twice a week, and then she married someone else and died within a year, sending for him at the end. Part III is called “Death.” An epoch is a marked period of time; sinewy means strong and lean; to meditate is to think deeply; “defiled” here means marched past in a line; custom means customers; an equipage is a carriage with horses; heliotropes are sweet-smelling purple flowers; unmanned means robbed of courage; plumes are feathers.
readings.contentNote: This part of the story, titled “Death,” tells of Will’s last night; on it the dead seem to return to him.

excerpt.locator: “Will o’ the Mill,” Part III, “Death,” from the start to the stranger crossing the courtyard; opens “Year after year went away into nothing, with great explosions and outcries in the cities…”; closes “…road behind the stranger, and, above that, a few black pine-tops, like so many plumes.”.

questions.prompt: What happens in the cities of the plain while Will stays in his valley? Why might Stevenson pack it all into one long sentence?
facilitatorNotes: Revolts, battles, new stars named, plays, hospitals: “all the usual turmoil.” The long list rushes past like the river, while the valley changes only with the seasons. The sentence makes the world’s noise and Will’s stillness felt at once.
evidence: red revolt springing up and being suppressed in blood
Up in Will's valley only the winds and seasons made an epoch

questions.prompt: Choose one of Will’s sayings and explain it. Do you agree with it?
facilitatorNotes: The dinner saying means that a long life saves its sweetest part for last, or perhaps that it does not; “I am a dead man now” means he no longer wants anything. The candle and the planet repeat his old idea that the unreachable makes near things sweeter. Any reading that explains the comparison is acceptable.
evidence: There is only one difference between a long life and a good dinner: that, in the dinner, the sweets come last.
he professed he had lived long enough to admire a candle all the more when he could compare it with a planet

questions.prompt: On the night he cannot sleep, what memories come back? How does Stevenson make them more than memories?
facilitatorNotes: The fat young man, his parents, Marjory: they come back to his “bodily senses.” He hears the dead miller call, smells Marjory’s heliotropes, and sees her window lit and the blind lifted as on the night he shouted to the stars. Ask readers which detail they recognise from earlier nights.
evidence: revisiting his bodily senses as they do in profound and vivid dreams
an overpowering sweetness of heliotropes

questions.prompt: Before the stranger even speaks, what tells the reader this is no ordinary night?
facilitatorNotes: The dead miller’s call, the impossible carriage on a dangerous pass at night, the dead seeming to crowd the courtyard, and pine-tops “like so many plumes,” the feathers worn by horses at a funeral. Readers who remember Will’s boyhood dream of a carriage at the door may guess where it will take him.
evidence: a few black pine-tops, like so many plumes
the voice of the dead miller calling to him out of the house

readings.title: Will o’ the Mill, part III — The stranger’s carriage
readings.challenge: Collect the hints that tell you who a character is before he names himself.
readings.focus: A stranger drinks a last bottle with Will and names himself, and the man who would never leave his valley at last goes down to the plain.
readings.context: Recap: Will, now seventy-two and famous for his quiet wisdom, has never left his mountain valley. On a stormy night he could not sleep; memories of the dead seemed real to him, he heard a carriage on the road, and a stranger crossed the courtyard towards him. To “tramp on people’s corns” is to offend them; a positive person is sure of his own opinions; a barouche is a carriage; febrile means feverish; a hare’s form is the hollow where it lies hidden; caustic means sharp-tongued; a physician is a doctor.
readings.contentNote: Death, as a character, comes for Will, and Will dies at the end of the story.

excerpt.locator: “Will o’ the Mill,” Part III, “Death,” from the stranger’s greeting to the end of the story; opens “"Master Will?" asked the new-comer, in brief military fashion.”; closes “…world rose next morning, sure enough Will o' the Mill had gone at last upon his travels.”.

questions.prompt: Why can Will not see the stranger’s face? Find two details that hint who he is before he names himself.
facilitatorNotes: Will makes out only “a shadow,” his heart grows cold, and the wine tastes odd. The stranger has crossed “kings and generals and great artists,” says he will take Will in his carriage “before this bottle's empty,” and touches him three times. Ask which hint readers caught first.
evidence: he could make out little more than a shadow at table with him
I have crossed the whims, in my time, of kings and generals and great artists

questions.prompt: Will boasts that “the devil himself could hardly root me up,” then says he is “tired enough of it all.” Which statement is truer?
facilitatorNotes: The first is the proud innkeeper; the second bursts out of him “in an explosive, febrile manner,” as if he has been holding it in. Readers may decide that his long contentment covered tiredness, or that both are honest at different depths.
evidence: I have grown here like an old oak-tree
God knows I am tired enough of it all

questions.prompt: How is Death in this story different from what you might expect?
facilitatorNotes: He is a doctor who takes away pain and forgives sins, a “natural law,” and he speaks to Will like a father who has been “yearning” for him. Will welcomes him as “the only friend I had to look for.” Some readers find this comforting; others find it sad that Will waited so long for him.
evidence: I take away all pain and I forgive all sins
I am a natural law

questions.prompt: The story ends: “Will o' the Mill had gone at last upon his travels.” How does this ending answer the boy who longed for the plain? Was his life well lived?
facilitatorNotes: The wind rushes “towards the plain,” and the carriage he dreamed of has come: he goes down the valley at last, in death. Some readers see a peaceful reward for a wise, quiet life; others see the irony of a man who waited for life until only death came. Ask students to use the whole story.
evidence: a rushing as of a smooth and steady wind descending towards the plain
Will o' the Mill had gone at last upon his travels.
